comments.rawMarkdown: I think that it is important to note that since humans can solve these problems directly without terrible effort we should focus a bit on why? I have long thought that domain knowledge in the form of previous human experience plays a key role (somewhat obvious). In many ways this is a challenge to see how actionable human-like experience can be transferred to the realm of AI efficiently. This is a surprisingly tricky problem. We try to approximate this experience with simple heuristics that make sense to us with respect to the problem domain but it is very difficult to truly recreate the "active" experiential knowledge that humans possess. What seems simple to us belies years of actual experience that we cannot fully consciously inspect. I think that a good world model coupled with a suitable agent framework and some clever heuristics could make great progress on this challenge.

I believe this is primarily a mapping problem. The model needs to predict potential future outcomes, similar to how humans consider their options before making a decision. By observing a situation, humans can often determine that taking a specific path, such as going right, may take less time. From my understanding, no existing architecture can adequately address this issue on its own. We need to redesign the system by integrating agentic behavior into the architecture. Currently, relying solely on foundational models and tools is not sufficient, in my opinion. I believe that a smaller model with a very structured architecture could potentially solve this problem entirely.
This competition might reshape the future of LLMs

I don't believe ARC-3 is a good test for AGI. In this sense:
All the puzzles rely on simple recognition of the problem + planning.

They don't involve having to have any "flash of insight". More like "flash of recognition". ARC-3 is more like "puzzle recognition".

e.g. the one with the water is just recognising having seen pixel water simulations before and recognising symbolic representation of cups.

That's all well and good but consider someone trying the "sliding-15" puzzle for the first time, this is more like AGI since we first explore moving about the tiles, then we formulate little theories about how to get each piece in place, and invent strategies.

I think the ARC-3 puzzles are too simple for real AGI. It is a small step in the right direction. Real AGI should be more focussed on the solving complicated tasks than the recognition IMO. I would prefer a blind genius AGI than a dumb seeing AI.

TLDR: An AI that can play chess well is better than an AI that can just recognise the game is called Chess.

comments.rawMarkdown: I think whether ARC is a mapping or sequential decision process depending on how much prior knowledge is already present in the agent's memory system. An navie (totally untrained) agent in the ARC games does not know why they are here, and what they expect, so at least in the first few each steps they will need to do decision->outcome->refine cognitive map -> next decision (sequential decision style). An expert agent, which have large amount of relevant knowledge, will directly recognize the step's place in its memory and find its corresponding next state, i.e. a mapping operation (o(1) in the most optimal case). However, I think when build a naive agent, if the structure design can reflect the mechanism of the game, i.e. the structure is prior knowledge, this could help the naive agent do one-shot or few-shot learning of the task

I posted kind of a book to a different thread, so I won't repeat all of it: [here](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/arc-prize-2026-arc-agi-3/discussion/688114#3436711) (in case you're curious).

But the TL;DR version (...comparatively :D) is that the hypothesis I've been working from is that the problem space (maybe/probably) requires managing information appropriateness, storage, and application of new learnings to help models compensate for not having a lifetime of playing games under their metaphorical belts.

The scoring makes it resource constrained, but my framing had been more along the lines of: when I play a game, what am I taking for granted? What do -I- need to play well, and how can I translate that... in a generalized way, of course (to avoid targeting specific mechanics and stuff)? How much information is too much information? 

In fact, my very first attempt (not submitted--unsure whether I'm going to join the competition, but it's an interesting space to explore), I tried out this hypothesis: "Could a smaller system with better structure outperform larger models on these tasks?"

The smallest models I tried needed so much handholding to produce anything remotely useful that I concluded it was going to be more effort than I had patience to make them primary. Think: encoding the scientific method into strict stages because I needed them to do better at reasoning than they had the capacity for. 

I'm experimenting with the size and type of models still, and I genuinely don't know whether my approach will work, which is part of the fun. But it's the framing I've gone with because I'm a systems person, and that's my jam. :) 

Good luck!

firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
I’ve been thinking about ARC-style tasks from a slightly different angle.

Most approaches seem to focus on pattern recognition, transformation rules, or model scaling. But I’m starting to wonder if we might be missing a more fundamental question:

What exactly do we mean by “intelligence” in this context?

If we look at these tasks from an agent perspective, intelligence might not just be about finding the correct transformation. It could also involve:

Allocating limited resources (time, compute, steps) efficiently
Avoiding unnecessary or high-risk operations
Recognizing when a current strategy is insufficient
Knowing when to explore vs exploit

In that sense, “being intelligent” might be less about being correct immediately, and more about how the system navigates uncertainty and constraints over time.

This raises a few questions I’d love to hear thoughts on:

Should ARC be treated as a static mapping problem, or as a sequential decision process?
How important is internal state representation compared to raw input-output matching?
Do current approaches sufficiently model uncertainty and failure modes?
Could a smaller system with better structure outperform larger models on these tasks?

Curious how others here are thinking about this - especially from a systems or agent design perspective.
